items.stem: Why is RAID not a substitute for backups?

options.text: RAID protects against drive failure but not deletion, corruption or ransomware
options.rationale: Correct: RAID adds availability, not recovery from logical data loss.

options.text: RAID copies data to an off-site location automatically
options.rationale: RAID is local redundancy, not an off-site copy.

options.text: RAID encrypts all data by default
RAID keeps historical versions of files
options.rationale: RAID does not retain previous versions.

items.explanation: Correct: RAID guards against drive failure but not deletion, corruption or ransomware.

items.stem: Which TWO statements describe the 3-2-1 backup principle? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Keep at least three copies of the data
options.rationale: Correct: three copies is the first part of 3-2-1.

options.text: Keep at least one copy off-site
options.rationale: Correct: an off-site copy survives a local disaster.

options.text: Keep every copy on the same server
options.rationale: Co-locating all copies defeats the purpose of 3-2-1.

options.text: Never test any of the copies
options.rationale: Testing restores is essential, not excluded.

items.explanation: Correct: 3-2-1 means three copies, on two media, with one off-site.

items.stem: Why should some backup copies be kept offline or immutable?

options.text: So ransomware that reaches the live data cannot also encrypt the backups
options.rationale: Correct: offline or immutable copies survive a ransomware attack.

options.text: Because offline copies restore faster than any other
options.rationale: Speed is not the reason; resilience is.

options.text: Because immutable backups need no retention policy
options.rationale: Retention is still required for immutable backups.

options.text: Because online backups cannot be encrypted at all
options.rationale: Online, writable backups can be encrypted by ransomware.

items.explanation: Correct: offline or immutable copies survive ransomware that hits live data.
